parts.title: The oldest tree in the village
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
In the middle of our village stands a huge oak tree. Nobody knows exactly how old it is, but people say that it is more than six hundred years old. Its trunk is so wide that five children can stand round it with their arms stretched out.

When I was small, the oak was the centre of everything. We played hide-and-seek among its roots, and in summer the whole village had picnics in its shade. My grandfather told me that, long ago, farmers held meetings under its branches.

Two years ago, a terrible storm broke one of the biggest branches. The villagers were very upset. Some people thought that the tree was dying and wanted to cut it down for safety. But an expert came from the city and examined it. He said that the oak was strong and healthy and would live for many more years.

Since then, we have taken better care of it. We built a low fence round the roots, to protect them from visitors' feet, and every spring, children come to measure it. Last year, I measured it with my own daughter, and she asked me, "Will it still be here when I am as old as you?" I hope so.

questions.prompt: How old is the oak thought to be?
questions.explanation: People say it is more than six hundred years old.

questions.prompt: What did the writer do under the tree as a child?
questions.explanation: They played hide-and-seek among its roots.

questions.prompt: Why were the villagers upset?
questions.explanation: A storm broke one of the biggest branches.

questions.explanation: He said the oak was strong and healthy.

questions.prompt: Why did the villagers build a fence?
questions.explanation: The fence protects the roots from visitors' feet.

parts.title: Why forests matter
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Forests cover almost one third of the land on Earth. [1] They are home to more than half of all the animals and plants that live on land.

Trees also help us breathe. [2] During the day, their leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and give back oxygen, which people and animals need.

Forests protect the soil too. [3] Without roots to hold the earth together, heavy rain can wash it away and cause floods.

Sadly, every year, millions of hectares of forest disappear. [4] Farmers, builders and companies cut them down to make space or to sell the wood.

However, there is some good news. [5] In many countries, people are planting new trees and creating protected areas where nothing may be cut down.
sentences: Nature is slowly beginning to recover in some places.
Wood from forests is also used to make paper and furniture.
Roots keep it firmly in place.
In autumn, the leaves of many trees turn red and gold.
The smaller trees grow faster than the large ones.
Large areas are lost for ever.
They are found on every continent except Antarctica.
The air in a forest is very clean.

gaps.explanation: Forests are found on every continent; the next sentence goes on with "They are home to" more than half of all animals and plants.
The air in a forest is clean; the next sentence says trees give back oxygen.
Roots keep the soil in place; the next sentence says without roots rain washes it away.
Large areas are lost for ever; the next sentence says farmers and builders cut them down.
Nature is recovering in some places; the next sentence says people are planting trees.

parts.title: A message from the woods
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Hi Nim, I am writing this from a camp in the middle of a forest. We arrived [1] Friday evening, and we put up our tents before dark. The air smells wonderful, [2] it is colder than I expected. Last night, we sat round a fire and [3] stories until midnight. This morning, I heard a strange noise. It was a deer, [4] was eating leaves near my tent! I wish you [5] here with us. We are staying until Sunday, so there is still time for you to [6] us. Auden

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: We use on with days of the week.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: But shows contrast: the air is lovely but cold.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: We tell stories, so the verb is told.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: Which is used for an animal in a relative clause.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: I wish you were here is the pattern for an unreal wish.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: Join us means to come and be with us.

parts.title: Planting a tree
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Planting a tree is a simple way to help the planet. First, choose a tree that suits your garden. Some trees grow very tall, [1] others stay small, so it is important to read the label. Dig a hole that is twice as wide as the roots. Put the tree in the hole and fill it [2] earth, pressing it down gently. Water it well, and keep watering it every week for the first year. Many people forget this, [3] their young trees die. It is also a good idea to put a stick next to the tree [4] hold it up in strong winds. In a few years, you will see birds visiting your tree, and one day, it may be [5] large that it gives shade in summer. Planting a tree is something [6] will be good for people for a hundred years.

gaps.explanation: While shows contrast between tall trees and small trees.
We fill a hole with earth.
So shows the result: people forget, so trees die.
A stick to hold it up gives the purpose.
So large that it gives shade.
That refers to something and begins the relative clause.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: This oak is enormous. The sign says it’s thirteen years old, but that can’t be right.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No, the sign is wrong. A guide told me that the path has been here for thirty years, and I think that’s where the mistake comes from. The tree itself is much older.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: How much older?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: It started to grow in seventeen twenty, so it’s three hundred years and a bit. That’s before the town even existed.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Incredible. Imagine everything that it has seen.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: And it still grows a little every year.

question.explanation: The sign (thirteen) is wrong and thirty years is the age of the path; the tree started to grow in seventeen twenty, so it is about three hundred years old.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Look! A squirrel on the path. It’s carrying something big, a stick, I think.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Hmm, it’s too small for that. Maybe it’s a leaf for its nest.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: No, look, it’s round and brown. It’s stopping to dig a hole.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: You’re right, it’s burying it. It’s saving food for the winter, like nuts and seeds.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I wish I could give it a sandwich, but my mum says not to feed the animals.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: She’s right. They find enough in the forest. Oh, it’s gone up the tree now.

question.explanation: The boy first guesses a stick and the girl a leaf, but the squirrel is carrying something round and brown that it buries as winter food, a nut.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Where shall we have our picnic? There’s the old oak by the lake, but we’d have to walk.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: The oak is very old, but I don’t mind that. I’d rather sit under the beech tree, next to the car park. We could keep the food in the car.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: True, but it’s a hot day.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That’s why I prefer the beech. Its leaves are so thick that the sun doesn’t reach the grass. We’ll be cool in the shade, and the children won’t get burnt.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Fine. I’ll bring the blanket.

question.prompt: Why does she choose the beech tree?
question.explanation: She says the oak is old and the car park is close, but she chooses the beech because its thick leaves keep the sun away and give shade.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Hi Zoe. About the school project on woodland jobs: you asked if my uncle could help. At first I thought of my uncle Ben, because he is a farmer, but his fields are ten kilometres from here, and he’s busy at this time of the year. My other uncle, Tom, used to teach in our school, but he doesn’t live here any more. Dad suggested Uncle Sam, who looks after the big forest by the river. He plants new trees, cuts the old ones and checks that they’re healthy. He says we can visit on Saturday morning. Call me back and tell me if that’s OK.

question.prompt: What does the uncle who will help with the project do?
question.explanation: Ben is a farmer who is too busy and Tom used to be a teacher, but Sam looks after the forest and plants and cuts trees, so he is a forester.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Excuse me, is it far to the lake?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Well, the sign at the gate says one hour, but that’s the long way round the hill. My dad and I go straight through the wood, and it takes us twenty minutes, because we stop to look at birds.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: That sounds good. Is it easy?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: There’s a steep bit at the start, but you look fit. If you walk quickly, you’ll be at the water in ten minutes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Great. Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Enjoy it. The lake is beautiful in the morning.

question.prompt: How long is the walk to the lake?
question.explanation: One hour is the sign for the long way and twenty minutes is the boy’s slow pace with his dad; the woman, who walks fast, needs ten minutes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Attention, all walkers. The path to the waterfall is closed today. Yesterday some people saw smoke near the car park, and we thought it was a small fire, but it was only a barbecue and it’s now out. Next month we’ll repair the bridge on the same path, but that work hasn’t started. The real reason is the storm last night. A large pine tree fell across the path near the second gate, and it’s too heavy to move by hand. A team with a chainsaw is coming tomorrow morning. Until then, please use the red path, which is longer but safe. Thank you.

question.explanation: The smoke was only a barbecue and the bridge repair is next month; the path is closed because a pine fell across it in the storm.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Excuse me, I want to make hot chocolate, but I’m not allowed to light a fire.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No fires, that’s right. Do you have a candle? Actually, don’t use that either, it’s dangerous in a tent.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I have a torch, but I need heat, not light.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Then go to the camp kitchen. There’s a gas stove with a blue button, and you can use it until nine.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Brilliant. Is it free?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes, but please wash the pan afterwards, and turn the gas off. Some campers forget, and then the next person finds a hot kitchen.

question.explanation: The boy cannot light a fire, the man rejects the candle, and the torch gives light but no heat; the camp kitchen has a gas stove that he can use.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Good morning. Can I help you?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I hope so. We’re planning a two-day walk, and I wondered if I could book a place on the campsite or a tour.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The campsite is full this weekend, I’m afraid, and the guided tours only run in summer.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Oh. Well, I don’t need a bed. I have a tent, and I’ll find somewhere. I just want to know which paths are open, and which are easy for my father, who is seventy.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Of course. Take this map. Avoid the north path, it’s steep. The lake path is flat.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: That’s exactly what I needed.

question.prompt: What does the woman want from the park office?
question.explanation: The campsite and the tours are not what she needs; she asks which paths are open and easy for her father, which is advice on routes.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: There are so many leaves in our garden. Dad wants to burn them.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Smoke is bad for the neighbours, and it’s not allowed here. My mum gives hers away to the farm for the animals’ beds.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The farm is too far, and Dad says they don’t take them now. But I have an idea for school. Our art teacher wants autumn pictures.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Oh yes, we can stick them on paper and paint around them. Great idea.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I’ll collect the best ones, the red and yellow.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I’ll bring the glue.

question.prompt: What do the two friends agree to do with the leaves?
question.explanation: Burning is bad and the farm is too far, so they decide to stick the leaves on paper for the art class.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Good morning, Mr Lane. I saw you cleaning the pond last week.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Oh, hello. Yes, somebody had to do it. Was my dog a problem?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Not at all. He’s lovely. I was going to say thank you, but then I thought of something better. We need volunteers on Saturday to plant trees, and you clearly like the park.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I’d love to, but I don’t have much experience.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Don’t worry, we show you everything. Bring gloves.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Count me in. Should I meet you at the pond, or at the main gate?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: At the main gate, at nine.

question.prompt: Why is the woman speaking to the man?
options: To ask him to help in the park
To say thank you for his work
question.explanation: The dog is not a problem and thanks was only her first idea; she invites him to plant trees on Saturday and he agrees.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Daniel, have you given me the form for the forest trip?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Not yet, Miss. I’m not sure if I can go. I thought it would cost a lot, like the museum trip last year.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: This time it’s free. The school pays for the bus, and we bring sandwiches.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Really? Then I’ll definitely come. I was afraid I’d have to stay in school, and I love the forest.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Good. And bring a coat, it’ll be cold.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I’ll ask my mum for the form tonight.

question.prompt: What was the boy worried about?
question.explanation: The teacher mentions the cold and the bus, but Daniel’s worry was the cost, like last year’s museum trip; the trip is free.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Look at all these nuts under the tree! Can we eat them? They look like chestnuts.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Be careful. Some are poisonous. Horse chestnuts aren’t safe, but these have spiky cases, so I think they’re sweet chestnuts.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Great, I’ll try one now.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Not raw! Grandma says they taste awful and can make you ill. We should cook them on the fire and then peel them.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: OK, you know more than me. Shall we give some to the birds?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: No, let’s keep them. They’re a treat.

question.prompt: What does the girl advise about the nuts?
options: Feed the nuts to the birds
question.explanation: She says they are probably safe but should not be eaten raw; she wants to cook them and rejects giving them to the birds.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Welcome to the forest. Shall we start with a photo by the entrance? Everyone does.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Maybe at the end. The light is better in the afternoon. I’m starving, but I’d rather eat later, once we’ve done the walk. First, the oak. I’ve read so much about it that I can’t wait to see it.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It’s twenty minutes along this path.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Perfect. Let’s go.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Don’t forget your boots. It’s wet.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I’ve got them on. Lead the way. I hope we see some deer on the way, I’ve never seen one in the wild.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Fingers crossed.

question.prompt: What does the woman want to do first?
question.explanation: Photos will be later in the afternoon and lunch after the walk; she is most eager to see the oak first.

parts.title: A radio message about a forest festival
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: presenter
turns.text: Welcome back to the afternoon show. This weekend, the town is holding its annual Forest Festival, and I can tell you everything you need to know. Last year we were in Mill Park, near the river, but it was too small, so this year the festival moves to Green Park, behind the library. The stall holders arrive at nine on Saturday, but the festival itself begins at ten in the morning. There’s music at twelve, and it finishes at six in the evening. On Sunday it starts a little later, at eleven. Now, the programme. There’ll be stories for children in the big tent, told by Mrs Dale, who teaches at the primary school. Mr Reed, the other storyteller, was ill, so he can’t come, but he sends his best wishes. In the green area, children can collect leaves and sticks and make nests for birds, and those will hang in the trees afterwards. If your children prefer masks, there’s a table for that too, but it’s smaller. And for the grown-ups, there is the sculpture competition. People have been making wooden animals for weeks. The winner will take home a hundred pounds. Last year the prize was only fifty, so it’s more exciting now. Entry is free, and there’s food, but I’d bring a bottle of water, because it will be hot. Parking is a problem, so please don’t bring your car. The number sixteen bus stops near the library, but it’s slow. The number six goes right to the main gate, and it runs every ten minutes. Finally, if it rains, the festival continues inside the sports hall. Remember to wear comfortable shoes, because the grass will be wet in the morning. Have a lovely weekend, and see you there!

gaps.prompt: This year the festival will be held in ___ Park
gaps.explanation: Last year it was in Mill Park, but this year it moves to Green Park.

gaps.prompt: The official start on Saturday is at ___ o'clock
gaps.explanation: The stall holders arrive at nine and the music is at twelve, but the festival begins at ten.

gaps.prompt: Stories for children will be told by Mrs ___
gaps.explanation: Mr Reed was ill, so the stories are told by Mrs Dale.

gaps.prompt: Children can use leaves and sticks to build ___ for birds
gaps.explanation: The masks table is smaller; children make nests from leaves and sticks.
Last year the prize was fifty pounds; now the winner takes home a hundred.

gaps.prompt: Visitors should take bus number ___ to the main gate
gaps.explanation: The number sixteen is slow and stops near the library; the number six goes to the main gate.

parts.title: An interview with a forest ranger
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tove, what is a normal day like for a forest ranger?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: There’s no such thing, really. People imagine that it’s very quiet, and sometimes it is, but then a visitor gets lost or a branch falls across the road. I never do the same thing two days in a row. In fact, that’s what I love about the work, because I’d go crazy in an office.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Which part of the day do you like most?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The early morning. The summer evenings are lovely, and the visitors are interesting, I meet them all day long. But at six, when the sun comes up, there is nobody here, only birds and the wind in the trees. That silence is the reason why I chose this job, and I still feel lucky every morning.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What annoys you most?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Well, dogs running free are a problem, mostly in spring, because many birds nest on the ground. The noise from the road is also bad on Sundays. But what really makes me angry is the rubbish. People leave bottles, bags and plastic everywhere, and the forest isn’t a bin.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Tell me about the snowstorm last winter. How did you feel?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I was alone in the north area when the snow started. A helicopter would have taken hours to arrive, and I didn’t climb a tree, that’s silly. I wasn’t frightened, and it wasn’t exciting either. I stayed calm because I knew what to do. I had trained for it three years before, and I remembered every step. I built a shelter with branches and sat inside until the morning.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice do you give visitors about mobile phones?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Some people think we should ban them, but I disagree. I don’t mind photos, they’re nice memories. The important thing is that the battery is full. If you hurt your leg, a phone is the only way for us to find you. So please charge it before you come, and tell somebody which path you are taking. I once found a family who had no idea where they were, and the phone saved the day.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And is it true that you say hello to a tree every day?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s true! There’s a beech near my office, about two hundred years old. I don’t plant a tree every day, that would be amazing, and my reports are very short. But I always stop and say good morning to it. People laugh, but it makes me smile, and it’s the best part of my walk to work.

questions.prompt: What does Tove say about her days?
questions.explanation: People imagine quiet days, but visitors get lost and branches fall; she never does the same thing two days in a row.

questions.prompt: Why does she like the early morning best?
questions.explanation: The summer evenings and the visitors are pleasant, but the silence at six with only birds is why she chose the job.

questions.prompt: What makes her most angry?
questions.explanation: Dogs and road noise are problems, but the rubbish that people leave makes her really angry.

questions.prompt: How did she feel in the snowstorm?
questions.explanation: She says she was not frightened and it was not exciting; she stayed calm because she knew what to do.

questions.prompt: What is her advice about phones?
questions.explanation: She does not want a ban and photos are fine, but the battery must be full so rangers can find an injured visitor.

questions.prompt: What does she do every day?
questions.explanation: She does not plant a tree daily and her reports are short; she stops and says good morning to the old beech.

parts.prompt: Your class is going to spend a day in a forest. Talk about the different activities that you could do and decide which would be the best.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Why do people feel calm in a forest?
What can ordinary people do to protect trees?
Is it better to live in a city or near nature? Why?
